L18: # OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0
L19: ## 【0†Abstract】
L20: 
L21: This document defines the Continuous Access Evaluation Profile (CAEP) of the Shared Signals Framework [【1†SSF】]. It specifies a set of event types conforming to the Shared Signals Framework. These event types are intended to be used between cooperating Transmitters and Receivers such that Transmitters may send continuous updates using which Receivers can attenuate access to shared human or robotic users, devices, sessions and applications.【2†¶】

L91: ## 【5†1.】 【6†Introduction】
L92: 
L93: CAEP is the application of the Shared Signals Profile of IETF Security Events 1.0 [【1†SSF】] (SSF Profile) to ensure access security in a network of cooperating providers. CAEP specifies a set of event-types that conform to the SSF Profile. This document specifies the event-types required to achieve this goal.【71†¶】
L94: ### 【7†1.1.】 【8†Notational Considerations】
L95: 
L96: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [【72†RFC2119】] [【73†RFC8174】] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.【74†¶】
L97: ## 【9†2.】 【10†Optional Event Claims】
L98: 
L99: The following claims are optional unless otherwise specified in the event definition.【75†¶】
L100: 
L101: event_timestamp【76†¶】
L102: 
L103:   * OPTIONAL, JSON number: the time at which the event described by this SET occurred. Its value is a JSON number representing the number of seconds from 1970-01-01T0:0:0Z as measured in UTC until the date/time.【77†¶】
L104: 
L105: initiating_entity【78†¶】
L106:   * OPTIONAL, JSON string: describes the entity that invoked the event. This MUST be one of the following strings:【79†¶】
L107: 
L108:     * `admin`: an administrative action triggered the event【80†¶】
L109: 
L110:     * `user`: an end-user action triggered the event【81†¶】
L111: 
L112:     * `policy`: a policy evaluation triggered the event【82†¶】
L113: 
L114:     * `system`: a system or platform assertion triggered the event【83†¶】
L115: 
L116: reason_admin【84†¶】
L117:   * OPTIONAL, JSON object: a localizable administrative message intended for logging and auditing. The object MUST contain one or more key/value pairs, with a BCP47 [【85†RFC5646】] language tag as the key and the locale-specific administrative message as the value.【86†¶】

L119:     {
L120:         "reason_admin": {
L121:             "en": "Landspeed Policy Violation: C076E82F",
L122:             "de": "Landspeed-Richtlinienverstoss: C076E82F",
L123:             "es-410": "Violacion de la politica de landspeed: C076E82F"
L124:         }
L125:     }
L126: 【87†Figure 1】: 【88†Example: Administrative reason information with multiple languages】
L127: 
L128: reason_user【89†¶】
L129:   * OPTIONAL, JSON object: a localizable user-friendly message for display to an end-user. The object MUST contain one or more key/value pairs, with a BCP47 [【85†RFC5646】] language tag as the key and the locale-specific end-user message as the value.【90†¶】

L131:     {
L132:         "reason_user": {
L133:             "en": "Access attempt from multiple regions.",
L134:             "de": "Zugriffsversuch aus mehreren Regionen.",
L135:             "es-410": "Intento de acceso desde varias regiones."
L136:         }
L137:     }
L138: 【91†Figure 2】: 【92†Example: End user reason information with multiple languages】
L139: ## 【11†3.】 【12†Event Types】
L140: 
L141: The base URI for CAEP event types is:【93†¶】
L142: 
L143: `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/caep/event-type/`【94†¶】
L144: ### 【13†3.1.】 【14†Session Revoked】
L145: 
L146: Event Type URI:【95†¶】
L147: 
L148: `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/caep/event-type/session-revoked`【96†¶】
L149: 
L150: Session Revoked signals that the session identified by the subject has been revoked. The explicit session identifier may be directly referenced in the subject or other properties of the session may be included to allow the receiver to identify applicable sessions.【97†¶】
L151: When a Complex Claim is used as the subject, the revocation event applies to any session derived from matching those combined claims.【98†¶】
L152: 
L153: The actual reason why the session was revoked might be specified with the nested `reason_admin` and/or `reason_user` claims described in 【99†Section 2】.【100†¶】
L154: #### 【15†3.1.1.】 【16†Event-Specific Claims】
L155: 
L156: There are no event-specific claims for this event type.【101†¶】
L157: 
L158: When `event_timestamp` is included, its value MUST represent the time at which the session revocation occurred.【102†¶】

L20: # Agent Passport System (APS): Verifiable Authority, Lifecycle, Enforcement, and Evidence for AI Agents
L21: ## 【0†Abstract】
L22: This document specifies the Agent Passport System (APS), a protocol for representing and evaluating authority exercised by AI agents. APS separates agent identity, represented principal, delegated authority, policy approval, admission to dispatch, observed results, and external effects.
L23: It defines cryptographic identity and principal records, monotonic delegation, revocation and authority-lifecycle semantics, deterministic action and decision references, signed governed-action records, verifier outcomes, evidence resolution, profiles, and protocol bindings.【1†¶】
L24: APS defines how an enforcement boundary rechecks current authority before admitting an action to dispatch, and how a verifier distinguishes what a signed record establishes from claims that remain unresolved or external to the protocol.
L25: Requirements are split into APS Core, which every conforming implementation carries, and Candidate features, which an implementation opts into by naming them in its claim, and most of the lifecycle and decision-to-effect material in this document is Candidate rather than Core. Candidate features specify additional lifecycle and decision-to-effect behavior without making those features requirements of APS Core conformance.【2†¶】
L26: Implementation and conformance sections identify which requirements have exact conformance-vector coverage and which are implemented by the reference implementations. APS does not treat a valid signature, receipt, or delegation chain as proof of external truth or of the absence of an out-of-band execution path.【3†¶】

L9: # Title:When Does Authorization End? Effect Closure at Provider Boundaries
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Igor Santos-Grueiro】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled When Does Authorization End? Effect Closure at Provider Boundaries, by Igor Santos-Grueiro
L14: 
L15: 【6†View PDF】 【7†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Revocation completion, clean state, or operation success can leave authorized work able to cause an effect the application rejects while the provider stays within its contract. We call the absence of all such paths policy-relative effect closure, or effect closure for short. Thus, a grant is closed when its existing authorizations retain no such path, and it cannot issue any new ones.
L17: > We present EFFECTBOUND, which uses an evidence-supported finite contract to decide whether an interface can truthfully report closure while required work completes. It reduces this to finite control with hidden state and returns a strategy, an impossibility certificate, or no verdict when evidence is insufficient. Machine-checked proofs establish the reduction and checker soundness; the checker derives closure results and validates certificates.
L18: Across GitHub, Kubernetes, NATS, and Kafka, closure fails in three ways: an interface lacks a needed control, clean visible state hides active work, or the model stops before the effect frontier---the last point where the effect can be prevented. The GitHub tool cannot bind a merge to the reviewed commit; a controlled run confirms that it may merge a different commit. NATS can report no stored or pending messages while dispatched work can still publish downstream.
L19: In Kafka, all fixed-set brokers had applied the revocation, yet an earlier authorized request could still append. We add a gate that blocks new use of revoked authority and delays return until earlier in-flight work completes. In a fixed-set Kafka~4.3.1 test deployment, this closes the studied synchronous, nontransactional write path without blocking unrelated requests. For a grant, authorization ends only when issuance stops and no earlier authorization can reach an effect the application rejects.
